title.en: St Olaf at Stiklestad: The Martyred King and the Shrine of Nidaros
title.zh: 斯蒂克勒斯塔德的聖奧拉夫：殉道國王與尼達羅斯聖龕

region.zh: 挪威斯蒂克勒斯塔德與尼達羅斯（特隆赫姆）

texts.period: Death 1030; Olafs saga helga (Heimskringla) c. 1225; Passio Olavi and the miracle-books (12th-13th c.); shrine at Nidaros

source.work: Snorri, Olafs saga helga chs. 200-206 (Stiklestad; the miracles); Passio et miracula Beati Olavi; English: Laing 1844

texts.license: Public domain (Laing 1844); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Olaf Haraldsson, king of Norway, falls at Stiklestad (1030) against the bonders' host; his body, buried in the sand by the river, is found incorrupt, the hair and nails grown, sweet-smelling - and the cult of the martyr-king explodes: the shrine at Nidaros (Trondheim), the miracles recorded in the Passio Olavi, the cures at the grave, the king made the saint of the kingdom. The record is the north's royal martyrdom: the death-battle as martyrdom, the incorruption as proof, and the shrine as the state's own sanctity.
summary.zh: 挪威國王奧拉夫·哈拉爾松於1030年在斯蒂克勒斯塔德對抗農民聯軍時陣亡；其遺體被葬於河邊沙中，後被發現屍身不朽、髮甲仍在生長、散發香氣——殉道國王的崇拜因此爆發：尼達羅斯（特隆赫姆）的聖龕、《聖奧拉夫受難錄》記錄的奇蹟、墓前的治癒之神蹟——國王成為王國的守護聖徒。此記錄是北方的王家殉道傳說：死戰即殉道，不朽即明證，聖龕即國家的神聖性。

texts.language: Old Norse / Old Icelandic; Latin (Passio Olavi)
texts.canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Passio Olavi per paraphrase

narrative.en:
The St-Olaf cycle is the north's royal martyrdom, and its doctrine is death-as-sanctity. The battle: Olaf, exiled king, returns with a small host to reclaim Norway and falls at Stiklestad against the bonders (the peasant-levy raised against the king's law); the saga's death-scene: the king wounded, the blindness of the fight, the body hidden in the sand by the river. The incorruption: the body is found a year later 'with? - the? - hair? - and? - nails? - grown, 'sweet? - smelling? - 'and? - 'the? - sand? - 'about? - it? - 'pure? - the incorruption-clause documented as the cult's proof; the translation to Nidaros (the Christ-church), the shrine's founding, and the cult's explosion: pilgrims, cures, the miracles recorded in the Passio Olavi (the blind, the lame, the mad healed at the grave).

The record's cultural functions are the martyr-king doctrine and the shrine-state doctrine: the king's violent death is read as martyrdom (the law-king killed by the lawless), and the shrine becomes the kingdom's own sanctity - the patron of Norway, whose cult the medieval state and church both served. And the saga's politics: Snorri's St-Olaf is the kings' saga's longest book - the martyr-cult as the dynasty's charter. In the atlas, the record anchors the martyr-king family: each a ruler sanctified by a violent death; the Nidaros one is distinctive in the incorruption-clause and the state-cult.

The battle's politics: Olaf returned from exile with a Swedish-Norwegian host and fell against the peasant-levy raised by the lords he had lawed against - the martyrdom's ambiguity documented in the saga itself, which records the bonders' case as well as the king's. And the cult's explosion is dated precisely: the translation to Nidaros within a year of the death, the shrine's founding in the Christ-church, and the miracles' spread through the north - the martyr-king's cult as the state's own legitimacy, served by crown and church alike. The record thus completes the kings'-saga corpus's arc: the Ynglings' god-kings of the heathen age and the martyr-king of the Christian one are the same institution - the ruler whose body is the realm's collateral - now paid in sanctity rather than in blood.

The battle's politics completes the doctrine: the bonders' host was raised by the lords the king had lawed against, and the saga records their case as well as the king's - the martyrdom's ambiguity is the saga's own honesty, the law-king killed by men who claimed law's cause. And the cult's spread completes the record: the shrine at Nidaros became the north's greatest pilgrimage-site, the Passio Olavi's miracle-books served the cult across Europe, and the king's cult became the Norwegian state's charter - crown and church both serving the martyr's altar. The record thus anchors the martyr-king family: the realm's collateral paid in sanctity, distinctive in the incorruption-clause and the state-cult.

functions: Martyr-king doctrine: the law-king's violent death read as martyrdom
Incorruption-clause: the body found grown and sweet-smelling as the cult's proof
Shrine-state: the Nidaros shrine as the kingdom's own sanctity
Miracle-record: the Passio Olavi's cures at the grave

title.en: Olaf Tryggvason's Missions: The Conversion-King and the Poet's Choice
title.zh: 奧拉夫·特里格瓦松的傳教：皈依之王與詩人的抉擇

region.en: Norway and the Norse west (symbolic pin at Trondheim)
region.zh: 挪威與北歐西部（象徵性定位於特隆赫姆）

texts.period: Reign 995-1000; Oddr Snorrason's Olafs saga Tryggvasonar (c. 1190); Hallfredar saga; Olafs saga Tryggvasonar en mesta

source.work: Oddr Snorrason, Olafs saga Tryggvasonar; Hallfredar saga; ed. Islenzk Fornrit VIII

texts.license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Olaf Tryggvason, the baptised viking-king, converts Norway and the Norse west by force and mission: the image-breaking, the forced baptisms, the missions to Iceland. And the sagas' finest episode is the poet's choice: Hallfred the troubadour? - the court-poet 'would? - not? - 'leave? - 'his? - 'faith? - 'with? - the? - 'old? - gods? - 'and? - the? - king? - 'grants? - 'him? - 'baptism? - 'and? - 'keeps? - 'his? - 'love? - the record is the conversion-king's portrait and the conversion-economy's cost as the poets documented it.
summary.zh: 受洗的維京國王奧拉夫·特里格瓦松以武力和傳教使挪威及北歐西部皈依：破除神像、強行施洗、派遣傳教團遠赴冰島。而薩迦最精彩的段落是「詩人的抉擇」：宮廷詩人哈爾弗雷德不願捨棄對舊神的信仰，國王卻為他施洗、並保全其愛情。此記錄是皈依之王的肖像，也是詩人筆下皈依經濟的代價。

texts.canonical_translation: Oddr Snorrason's saga per paraphrase; Hallfredar saga in Islenzk Fornrit VIII

narrative.en:
The Tryggvason-missions are the conversion-economy's political narrative, and the sagas' finest episode is its human cost. The missions: the king converts Norway 'by? - 'fire? - and? - 'baptism? - (the image-breaking at the temples, the forced baptisms at the feasts) and sends missionaries to Iceland and the west (the Thangbrand mission of the Icelandic record); the saga-portrait: the king as the conversion's enforcer and its martyr-figure (he falls at Svolder, 1000, the year of Iceland's conversion - the sagas' paired dates).

The poet's choice: Hallfredr, the court-skald, 'would? - 'not? - 'renounce? - 'his? - 'faith? - 'with? - the? - old? - gods? - 'and? - the? - king? - 'says: 'then? - 'be? - 'baptized? - 'and? - 'keep? - 'thy? - 'love? - 'the? - conversion-contract: baptism accepted, love kept - the poet converts on the terms of his own heart (the saga's clause: he keeps his beloved in Iceland), and the conversion-economy's cost is the poet's biography - the skald caught between the old gods' verse and the new king's faith.

The record's cultural functions are the conversion-enforcer doctrine and the poet's-choice doctrine: the mission-king's violence documented as the north's conversion-mechanism, and the poets' conversion-costs as the record's human ledger. In the atlas, the record anchors the mission-king family: each a ruler converting by force; the Tryggvason one is distinctive in the poets' testimonies.

The missions' enforcement is documented in its costs: the image-breaking at the Norse temples (the saga's burning of the hof at Trondheim), the forced baptisms at the assemblies, and the missionaries' violence abroad (Thangbrand's killings in Iceland). And the record's finest human document is the poets': Hallfredr's conversion-contract (baptism for love kept), and the sagas' testimony that the skaldic art survived conversion intact - the mead-myth's craft outlasting its gods. The conversion-economy's ledger thus runs both ways: the king's force converts the north, and the poets' craft converts the force into literature - the Tryggvason-missions documented as both politics and poetry.

The king's saga-frame completes the doctrine: the Tryggvason-cycle is the conversion-economy's founding narrative, and its finest literary product is the poets' testimony - Hallfredr's contract (baptism for love kept) and the skalds' survival of the conversion with their craft intact, the mead-myth's art outlasting its gods. And the missions' geography completes the record: Norway, Iceland, the Faroes, Shetland and Orkney converted in one reign's program - the north's faith-change as a single political operation, documented king by king and farm by farm. The record thus anchors the mission-king family: the ruler as the conversion's enforcer, distinctive in the poets' ledger of its costs.

functions: Conversion-enforcer doctrine: the mission-king's fire-and-baptism method documented
Poet's-choice doctrine: the skald's conversion-contract (baptism accepted, love kept)
Conversion-economy: the missions to Iceland and the west
Svolder-1000 pairing: the king's fall and Iceland's conversion as one date

passages.note: Paraphrase of Hallfredar saga (Islenzk Fornrit VIII); not verbatim.

title.en: Gudmundr the Good: Iceland's Wonder-Working Bishop
title.zh: 「善者」古德蒙德：冰島行奇蹟的主教

region.en: Holar and the north of Iceland

texts.period: Gudmundar saga biskups (13th-14th c., A and B versions); d. 1237; local cult of the 'holy Gudmundr'

source.work: Gudmundar saga biskups (A and B versions); ed. Biskupa sogur III (Islenzk Fornrit XVIII)

texts.license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Gudmundr Arason, bishop of Holar (1203-1237), is Iceland's folk-saint of the common people: a bishop of charity (he gave away the see's goods), of exorcisms (the ghosts bound by his mass), and of posthumous miracles (the cures at his mound at? - the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - the record is the folk-saint's saga: the wonder-working bishop whose cult ran outside the church's formal canonization.
summary.zh: 霍拉主教古德蒙德·阿拉松（1203-1237在任）是冰島平民的民間聖徒：一位慈善主教（散盡教座財物）、驅魔主教（以彌撒縛鬼），死後更顯奇蹟（墳前治癒之說不絕）。此記錄是民間聖徒的薩迦：一位行奇蹟的主教，其崇拜在教會正式冊封之外自發流傳。

texts.canonical_translation: Biskupa sogur III, Islenzk Fornrit XVIII; paraphrase

narrative.en:
The Gudmundr-saga is the folk-saint's biography, and its doctrine is charity-as-sanctity. The bishop's career: consecrated bishop of Holar in 1203, he gave away the see's goods to the poor (the charity-clause that the church's officials disputed), fought the powerful with the poor's claims, and - the saga's supernatural register - performed exorcisms (the ghosts bound by his mass) and cures. The posthumous cult: after his death (1237), the cures at his grave and mound were recorded in the saga's later chapters - the folk-cult of the 'holy Gudmundr', which ran outside the formal canonization (never canonized, venerated for centuries).

The record's cultural functions are the folk-saint doctrine and the charity-sanctity doctrine: the wonder-worker whose sanctity is measured in the poor's relief, and whose cult is the people's own - the Icelandic church's popular canonization, documented in the saga's miracle-chapters. In the atlas, the record anchors the folk-saint family: each a locally venerated wonder-worker; the Icelandic one is distinctive in the never-canonized status.

The saga's B-version expands the posthumous cult in detail: the cures at the mound, the visions of the poor at the grave, and the bishop's own intervention in the household crises of the north - the folk-saint as the region's ongoing patron rather than a past event. And the record's institutional irony is the saga's own: the formal church never canonized Gudmundr, while the people's cult ran for centuries - the Icelandic church's canonization process and its popular counterpart ran in parallel, and the saga preserves both voices: the bishops' discipline and the household's devotion. In the folk-cult's economy, the wonder-worker's authority is measured in the poor's testimony - the same ledger the seeress-profession kept, but in Christian coin.

The bishop's conflicts complete the doctrine: the saga records his disputes with the powerful chiefs and with the church's own officials (the goods-giving disputed as mismanagement), so the folk-saint's career is documented in both registers - the bishops' discipline and the people's devotion. And the posthumous cult's geography completes the record: the cures at his grave at Holar and at his mound, the visions of the poor, the local feast-days kept into the modern era - the never-canonized cult's continuity documented from the saga to the present. The record thus anchors the folk-saint family: sanctity measured in the poor's relief, distinctive in the cult's extra-institutional persistence. And the record's documentary form completes the corpus: the A-version's political biography and the B-version's miracle-register preserve both the historian's and the people's Gudmundr - the folk-saint whose authority is the poor's testimony, documented in the saga's two voices and in the cult's centuries of unbroken local practice.

functions: Folk-saint doctrine: the popular cult running outside formal canonization
Charity-sanctity: the bishop's goods given to the poor as sanctity
Exorcism-office: the ghosts bound by the bishop's mass
Posthumous cures: the mound and grave as the cult's sites
